items.q: The RabbitMQ model: exchange, queue, binding, routing key?
items.a:
The producer sends a message to an [[b:exchange]] → the exchange routes it into a [[b:queue]] via a [[b:binding]] + routing key.

**Exchange types:**
- direct (exact match)
- topic (wildcard)
- fanout (broadcast)
- headers

RabbitMQ is a [[g:'smart broker, dumb consumer']] — the broker owns routing and message state.

:::deep
- [[b:direct]]: routing key matches exactly (dispatch by type)
- [[b:topic]]: wildcard `*`/`#` (e.g. `booking.*.created`)
- [[b:fanout]]: broadcasts to every bound queue (pub/sub)
- [[b:headers]]: matches on headers

Durability: only *durable queue* + *persistent message* + *quorum queue* (Raft, replacing the old mirrored queue) survives a node loss.

OTA: a topic exchange routes `payment.succeeded`/`booking.cancelled` to several consumers (ticketing, notification, loyalty); a priority queue handles OTP/urgent transactions.

[[r:a long queue (backlog) means consumers can't keep up]] → scale consumers or raise prefetch.
:::

items.q: The Kafka model: topic, partition, offset, consumer group?
items.a:
Kafka is an immutable [[g:distributed log]]:
- a [[b:topic]] is split into [[b:partition]]s
- each message has a monotonically increasing [[b:offset]] within its partition
- consumers in the same [[b:consumer group]] split the partitions between them (one consumer per partition) → parallel scaling

[[g:'Dumb broker, smart consumer']] — the consumer manages its own offset. Messages are kept per retention (not deleted on read) → [[g:replayable]].

:::deep
- messages are kept per [[b:retention]] (time/size), NOT deleted on read → multiple consumer groups can read independently and replay (by resetting the offset)
- each partition is handled by one consumer within a group (useful consumer count ≤ partition count)
- committing the offset means 'processed up to here' → commit *after* processing (at-least-once), never auto-commit before processing

OTA: Kafka acts as the event backbone (booking CDC → search/loyalty/analytics, immutable audit, event-sourcing ledger); size partitions for throughput and consumer count ([[r:reducing partition count later is hard]] → over-provision moderately).

Key = `booking_id` to preserve event order for a given booking.
:::

items.q: RabbitMQ vs Kafka — when do you use which?
items.a:
RabbitMQKafka
Modelsmart broker (queue)distributed log
After readingmessage disappears (ack)kept per retention → replay
Routingflexible (exchange)partitioned by key
Throughputhighextremely high (millions of msg/s)
Good fortask queues, RPC, command dispatchevent streams, sourcing, analytics
:::tip Bottom line RabbitMQ = a task queue with smart routing; Kafka = a durable distributed log with replay and high throughput. Many systems use both. ::: :::deep - [[g:RabbitMQ]] when you need flexible routing, task queues/RPC, low latency for discrete work, per-message TTL/priority, 'send a command to a consumer' - [[g:Kafka]] when you need massive throughput, storage & replay, multiple independent consumers, event sourcing/log pipelines/analytics, partition-scoped ordering [[r:Don't force one broker to do everything.]] OTAs typically use BOTH: Kafka as the event bus/CDC/analytics backbone, RabbitMQ for routed tasks (dispatching tickets through a provider, retry jobs). :::

items.q: What do the delivery semantics at-most-once / at-least-once / exactly-once mean?
items.a:
Delivery semantics describe what may happen to one logical delivery across retries and acknowledgements [[o:inside a stated boundary]]. They do not by themselves guarantee disk durability, infinite retention, producer correctness, or an external side effect.
SemanticTypical protocol behaviorApplication consequence
at-most-oncedo not retry, or acknowledge/commit before processinga failure may lose work; the delivery protocol does not intentionally redeliver it
at-least-onceretry/redeliver until an acknowledgement within the broker's availability and retention policythe handler may run more than once, so effects need idempotency/deduplication
exactly-once within a scopededuplicate or atomically commit input position and output/state under a defined transaction modelno duplicate committed result inside that scope; external systems remain outside unless they join the same protocol
For one flow, name three boundaries separately: producer → broker acceptance, broker → consumer delivery/ack, and consumer → state/side effect. A protocol can be at-least-once at one boundary while the business effect is lost because the consumer acknowledged before committing—or duplicated because it committed then crashed before acknowledging. :::deep Kafka transactions can provide scope-bound exactly-once read-process-write behavior for supported Kafka records/state; they do not atomically include an arbitrary payment provider or database. RabbitMQ redelivery plus a database inbox can make the database effect converge, but the ack and database transaction are still distinct. “Effectively once” is an application outcome: durable identity, at-least-once recovery, atomic deduplication with the protected state change, deterministic response and sufficient retention. State the failure model instead of claiming either “exactly once everywhere” or “exactly once is impossible.” Consumer implementation is in (08-message-queue.reliability-delivery-semantics.q6), with scope examples in (25-microservice.03-distributed-data-consistency.q5). :::

items.q: How do RabbitMQ Publisher Confirms and consumer ack/prefetch work?
How does Kafka guarantee durability: replication, ISR, acks?
items.a:
Kafka durability is defined per partition and acknowledged record: - a partition has a leader and replicas; the [[b:ISR]] is the set currently considered in sync - `acks=0` does not wait, `acks=1` waits for the leader, and `acks=all` waits for the current in-sync replica set according to broker semantics - `min.insync.replicas` sets the minimum ISR size required to accept an `acks=all` write; below it, writes fail instead of silently weakening the policy - replication factor defines placement count, while rack/zone awareness and unclean-leader-election policy define important parts of the failure model 
# Illustrative policy; validate against broker count, zones and availability target.
replication.factor=3
min.insync.replicas=2
acks=all
enable.idempotence=true
This commonly tolerates one broker failure when the required replicas and storage remain healthy; it is not a promise against correlated zone/storage loss, operator error, retention, or every acknowledgement ambiguity. Idempotent producer mode prevents duplicate log appends from supported producer retries and is enabled by default in modern clients when no conflicting setting disables it—pin and verify the client configuration. :::deep Committing a consumer offset after an external side effect gives at-least-once behavior: a crash between effect and commit repeats. Committing first risks loss. Kafka transactions can atomically commit consumed offsets with produced Kafka records for supported read-process-write flows, but a normal external database/PSP remains outside. Ordering is per partition; key choice, producer concurrency, retries and partition-count migration matter (08-message-queue.reliability-delivery-semantics.q4). Monitor ISR shrink, under-replicated/offline partitions, produce error/latency and consumer lag, then rehearse broker/zone loss instead of treating a three-number recipe as durability proof. :::

items.q: Ordering: how do the two brokers guarantee it?
items.a:
Ordering must be scoped to a key and an observable effect.
KafkaRabbitMQ
broker orderappend order within one partitionqueue order, subject to delivery/redelivery and queue features
parallelismdifferent partitions can progress independentlycompeting consumers receive work concurrently; single-active-consumer can serialize active delivery
application riskproducer races, key/partition changes, retries, rebalance and parallel handlersrequeue/redelivery, multiple consumers and handlers completing out of order
For Kafka, use the aggregate ID as a stable key only when all events sharing the invariant use the same partitioning contract. With producer idempotence enabled, supported in-flight/retry configurations preserve partition order; with it disabled, retries and multiple in-flight batches can reorder. Increasing partition count can move future records for a key, so plan migration or rely on aggregate versions rather than historical physical contiguity. For RabbitMQ, one queue/consumer lane narrows ordering, and single-active-consumer provides active/standby consumption, but a crash/redelivery can repeat work. Broker delivery order does not force database side effects from asynchronous handlers to finish in that order. :::deep When stale/out-of-order application is harmful, include an aggregate sequence/version and apply it with an atomic condition; define gap handling, duplicate handling and replay. Event timestamps from distributed producers do not create total order. A global single partition/consumer sacrifices availability/throughput and still cannot atomically order arbitrary external systems. Test producer retry, two producers for one key, rebalance/failover, delayed old event, poison-message bypass and DLQ replay. The quick operational card is (25-microservice.04-messaging-event-driven-at-scale.q2). :::

items.q: DLQ and poison messages — how are they handled?
items.a:
A message that keeps failing ([[r:poison]]) blocks the queue if retried forever.

- after N failures → move it to a [[g:Dead-Letter Queue]] so it doesn't clog the main flow → investigate/fix/replay
- retry with exponential backoff + jitter, with a retry limit
- Kafka: retry topic + DLT

:::warn Interview trap
Two follow-up questions usually trip people up. *'Where does the retry live?'* — retrying inline in the consumer blocks the rest of the partition behind it, which is why Kafka needs a separate retry topic.
:::

*'How do you safely replay from a DLQ?'* — replay is only safe when the consumer is idempotent (08-message-queue.reliability-delivery-semantics.q6); otherwise every redrive charges the customer again.
:::deep
- pattern: retry with *exponential backoff + jitter* via a retry topic (Kafka) or TTL + dead-letter-exchange (RabbitMQ); after N attempts → DLQ (needs redrive tooling)
- distinguish [[o:transient]] errors (retryable — network) from [[r:permanent]] ones (straight to DLQ — bad schema)
- track DLQ size as an [[g:SLO]] (a growing DLQ signals a systemic bug)

OTA: a 'ticket issuance' message that fails permanently must go to the DLQ and alert an operator (it affects a customer) — [[r:never drop it silently]].
:::

items.q: Idempotent consumer — how do you implement dedup?
items.a:
At-least-once can deliver duplicates → the consumer must detect and skip them:
- a [[b:message id/business key]] + a 'processed' table (unique constraint) written in the *same transaction* as the business effect
- or use operations that are inherently idempotent (UPSERT, setting absolute state)

Kafka also offers an idempotent producer + transactions for 'exactly-once within Kafka's own scope'.

:::tip Bottom line
consumer-side idempotency is a survival requirement for any reliable messaging system — never assume 'each message is processed exactly once'.
:::

:::deep
Two approaches:
- [[g:inherently idempotent operations]] (UPSERT, setting absolute state) — simplest option when it applies
- [[g:dedup table]] with a unique constraint on message-id/business-key, written in the *same transaction* as the business effect ([[r:splitting them leaves a gap where the effect happened but wasn't marked yet]])

OTA: the consumer that 'awards loyalty points' on `payment.succeeded` must be idempotent (the same `payment_id` awards points only once) — a unique `(payment_id)` in a processed table, written in the same tx as the points update.
:::

items.q: The Outbox pattern with a message queue — why is it needed?
items.a:
[[r:Dual write]] (write to the DB, then publish) isn't atomic → the two sides fall out of sync if either one fails. [[g:Outbox]]: write the event into an outbox table in the *same transaction* as the business change; a separate publisher (polling or CDC/Debezium) reads the outbox, publishes, and marks it sent. 
BEGIN;
  UPDATE wallet SET balance=balance-100 WHERE id=?;
  INSERT INTO outbox(type,payload,status) VALUES('DEBITED',?,'PENDING');
COMMIT;  -- publisher -> broker -> mark SENT (at-least-once)
Only combining [[g:Publisher Confirms]] (broker received it) with [[g:Outbox]] (DB↔publish atomicity) closes the gap completely. :::deep - dual-write (writing to the DB then publishing to the broker as separate steps) is NOT atomic → a crash between the two steps leaves them inconsistent (the DB says the money moved but the event never went out, or vice versa) - [[g:Outbox]]: write the event into an outbox table in the *same transaction* (DB-local atomicity); a separate publisher (polling, or CDC/Debezium reading the binlog) emits it to the broker and marks it SENT (at-least-once → consumer must be idempotent) OTA: when a booking transitions to PAID, write the state change and a 'PaymentSucceeded' outbox row in one tx → the publisher fans it out to ticketing/notification/loyalty; [[r:never 'write to the DB then call Kafka' directly inside business logic]]. - On the domain side of that same outbox table: what gets published externally is an [[b:integration event]] — a public contract that must be versioned — distinct from an internal domain event (24-domain-driven-design.tactical-modelling-it.q3). :::

items.q: Event-driven architecture & event sourcing — concepts and trade-offs?
items.a:
- [[b:Event-driven]]: services communicate via async events → decoupling, scale, resilience
- [[b:Event sourcing]]: the *sequence of events* is the source of truth instead of current state; state = replaying events

**Benefits:** perfect audit trail, time travel, rebuildable views (a great fit for fintech/ledgers).

**Trade-offs:** added complexity, eventual consistency, event versioning, needs [[o:CQRS]] for efficient reads.

:::deep
- [[b:event-driven]] gives decoupling/scale/resilience but makes [[r:reasoning about the overall flow harder]] (logic is scattered across consumers), brings eventual consistency, and needs strong observability (tracing across events)
- [[b:event sourcing]]: state = replay → perfect audit trail, time travel, rebuildable read models; the trade-off is complexity (event versioning/upcasting, snapshots for fast replay, requires CQRS)

OTA: the ledger and a booking's lifecycle are good candidates (every change is an immutable event → easy reconciliation/audit/rebuild); [[r:don't event-source everything]] — event-sourcing simple CRUD is over-engineering.

- Distinguish domain events (internal, free to change) from integration events (public contracts) before committing to event-driven design; conflating the two is the hardest kind of hidden coupling to untangle later (24-domain-driven-design.tactical-modelling-it.q3).
:::

items.q: Your consumer group rebalances every few minutes and reprocesses messages. Which settings cause that, and how do you stop it?
items.a:
A Kafka consumer proves it is alive two different ways, and confusing them is the usual cause of a rebalance loop. - the [[g:heartbeat thread]] runs in the background and answers `session.timeout.ms` - the [[g:poll loop]] itself must return within `max.poll.interval.ms`, which is what your processing time is measured against So a consumer stuck processing a batch keeps heartbeating — it looks alive — until the poll interval expires, the coordinator declares it dead, and the partitions move. 
poll() returns 500 records → handler needs 6 min → max.poll.interval.ms = 5 min
        → coordinator evicts the consumer → rebalance
        → partitions reassigned, offsets never committed
        → the whole batch is delivered again, to someone else
SettingControlsTune when
`max.poll.records`batch size per pollprocessing per record is slow — lower it first
`max.poll.interval.ms`allowed processing time per batchwork is genuinely long-running
`session.timeout.ms` + `heartbeat.interval.ms`liveness detectionnetwork is flaky; heartbeat ≈ 1/3 of session
`fetch.min.bytes` / `fetch.max.wait.ms`batching vs latencythroughput matters more than a few ms
`partition.assignment.strategy`eager vs cooperativealways prefer cooperative — it stops the world far less
**The fix is usually not a bigger timeout.** Shrink the batch, move slow work off the poll thread, or `pause()` the partitions while a downstream is struggling and `resume()` after — that is backpressure applied where it belongs (25-microservice.04-messaging-event-driven-at-scale.q1). :::warn Every rebalance is a duplicate-delivery event Offsets not yet committed are redelivered to the new owner. That is exactly why the handler must be idempotent rather than merely careful (08-message-queue.reliability-delivery-semantics.q6). ::: :::deep - commit [[o:after]] processing, never before, and prefer manual commits. Auto-commit fires on a timer and can acknowledge records your handler has not finished. - adding consumers beyond the partition count adds idle members, not throughput. Parallelism is bounded by partitions (08-message-queue.the-two-models.q2). - running several threads per partition regains throughput but loses per-key ordering unless you shard by key inside the consumer (25-microservice.04-messaging-event-driven-at-scale.q2). - alert on both [[b:lag and the age of the oldest unprocessed record]]. Lag alone looks fine on a low-traffic topic where a message has been stuck for an hour (20-observability-sre.slos-alerting-incidents.q2). - a static group membership id lets a restarting pod keep its partitions across a short outage, which removes the rebalance from every deploy. :::

items.q: An event is a published contract you cannot recall. How do you design and evolve one without breaking consumers you do not control?
items.a:
A REST response is read once by the caller in front of you. An event sits in a log for its whole retention and is read by services that did not exist when you published it. **Design decisions that outlive the code:** - [[g:event, not command]] — `OrderConfirmed` states a fact that already happened; `ConfirmOrder` is an instruction addressed to someone. Facts can have many readers, instructions cannot - [[g:fat or thin]] — carrying the data makes consumers independent but exposes your model; carrying only an id forces a callback and a race, because the reader may fetch a state newer than the event - [[g:key by the entity]] the ordering is defined on, since ordering exists only inside a partition (08-message-queue.reliability-delivery-semantics.q4) - [[g:no PII you cannot delete]] — retention keeps it, replicas copy it, and a replay resurrects it (13-security-oauth2.protecting-the-data-you-store.q3)
Compatibility modeGuaranteesPick it when
BACKWARDnew readers read old dataconsumers deploy first — the common default
FORWARDold readers read new dataproducers deploy first
FULLboth directionsrolling deploys where order is not controlled
NONEnothingnever, on a shared topic
The registry enforces this at build time; which mode is correct follows directly from [[o:who deploys first]]. For the field-level rules — additive is safe, removal and renames are not — see the compatibility table in (26-testing-strategy.integration-tests-that-tell-the-truth.q4). :::tip When a change cannot be made compatible Publish a new topic or an explicitly versioned event type, dual-publish for one migration window, move consumers over, then retire the old one. Rewriting history in place is not available to you. ::: :::deep - version the [[b:schema, not the payload]]: a `version` field inside the body forces every consumer to branch. The registry already carries the writer's schema id per record. - consumers should tolerate unknown fields and unknown enum values — reading an unrecognised status as a fallback constant is the difference between an outage and a log line. - a [[r:log compacted]] topic is a state store: the key must be the entity id, and a `null` value is the tombstone that deletes it — which is also the only way to erase a subject from the topic. - events describing internal aggregate structure leak the domain model across a boundary; publish an integration event shaped for outsiders (24-domain-driven-design.tactical-modelling-it.q3). - record consumer expectations as contract tests in CI so a producer learns which fields anyone actually reads before it removes one (25-microservice.08-operational-concerns.q1). :::
